Where it began

Greg Chappell was born in Unley, South Australia, on 7 August 1948, the middle one of three brothers who all played Test cricket for Australia: Ian was the eldest and Trevor the youngest. His father Martin, a respected Adelaide club cricketer, had him holding a bat almost as soon as he could walk, and his mother's father was Vic Richardson, a former Australia captain.

Small for his age, he coped with bouncing deliveries by hitting mostly to leg. A growth spurt in his teens made him tall, and at 18 he made his first-class debut for South Australia. Two seasons with Somerset turned him from a leg-spinner into a medium-pacer.

The player

He made a hundred on his Test debut, against England at Perth in 1970–71. In 87 Tests between 1970 and 1984 he scored 7,110 runs at 53.86, with 24 hundreds, 31 fifties and a best of 247 not out. He held 119 catches and led Australia in 48 Tests, winning 21, losing 13 and drawing 14.

His 131 at Lord's in 1972, the innings he rated his best, helped Australia level an Ashes series. At Wellington he made 247 not out and 133, then a record 380 runs in one Test, while Ian also made hundreds in both innings. In his first Test as captain, against West Indies at Brisbane, he scored a century in each innings. And he signed off in January 1984 with 182, so his Test career began and ended with a hundred, something no batsman had managed before.

What made him special

Chappell batted tall and calm. Early on he got out chasing big shots, so he devised the Chappell vee: until he was settled, he kept his shots inside a narrow V from mid-off round to mid-on. When Don Bradman suggested a new grip to help his off-side play, he changed it straight away.

He was a superb catcher too. At Perth in 1974–75 he took seven catches in a Test, a new world record for a fielder, and one of the men whose record of six he beat was his own grandfather. His medium pace was more of a useful extra: 47 wickets at a little over 40 apiece suggest it was best kept as a pleasant surprise for tired batsmen.

Away from the middle

Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1973. After retiring he became a national selector and a member of the Australian Cricket Board, coached South Australia and commentated for Channel 9 and ABC radio. His honours include an MBE in 1979, appointment as Officer of the Order of Australia in 2021, and places in the Sport Australia Hall of Fame and, from 2002, the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame.

And finally

Brothers who grow up playing backyard cricket rarely let each other win, and the Chappell games were famously fierce. At the Oval in 1972 Greg and Ian became the first brothers to make Test hundreds in the same innings, which must have settled a few backyard arguments, or started new ones.
